questions.explanationCorrect: Streaming is recommended for long outputs or high max_tokens to avoid HTTP timeouts, and the SDK's get_final_message()/finalMessage() gives you the fully assembled message.
questions.explanationDistractor: Lowering max_tokens (A) sacrifices the output you actually need; streaming solves the timeout without truncating the response.

questions.stem: You need the model's final response to conform exactly to a JSON schema so a downstream service can parse it without defensive code. On current models, what is the recommended mechanism?

options.A: Prefill the assistant message with an opening brace to force JSON
options.B: Ask for JSON in the prompt and hope it complies
options.C: Use output_config.format with a JSON schema to constrain the response, and strict: true on a tool to guarantee valid tool arguments
options.D: Post-process the text with a JSON-repair library

questions.explanationCorrect: Structured outputs via output_config.format with a JSON schema constrain the response to valid JSON, and strict: true guarantees valid tool arguments; this replaces the old prefill trick.
questions.explanationDistractor: Assistant-message prefills (A) return a 400 on current models and are no longer the way to force JSON; structured outputs are the supported mechanism.

questions.stem: In the Model Context Protocol, which trio names the core primitives a server can expose?

options.A: prompts, embeddings, and fine-tunes
options.B: endpoints, webhooks, and secrets
options.C: agents, workflows, and pipelines
options.D: tools, resources, and prompts

questions.explanationCorrect: MCP servers expose three core primitives: tools, resources, and prompts.
questions.explanationDistractor: Embeddings and fine-tunes (A) are not MCP primitives; the correct trio is tools, resources, and prompts.

questions.stem: You are connecting Claude to a local MCP server running on the same machine and, separately, to a remote hosted one. Which transports fit these two cases?

options.A: stdio for the local server and streamable HTTP/SSE for the remote server
options.B: HTTP for the local server and stdio for the remote server
options.C: WebSocket for both, since MCP requires it
options.D: gRPC for the local server and REST for the remote server

questions.explanationCorrect: MCP uses stdio for local servers and streamable HTTP/SSE for remote ones.
questions.explanationDistractor: Option B reverses the two: stdio is the local transport and HTTP/SSE is for remote servers, not the other way around.

questions.stem: A team wants Claude to run an agent loop with tool execution, context management, and file/permission handling largely handled for them, rather than writing that orchestration against raw HTTP. Which choice matches?

options.A: The raw Messages API, because it already includes an agent harness
options.B: The Claude Agent SDK, which provides the harness (loop, tool execution, context handling) on top of the API, whereas the raw Messages API gives you the primitives to build that yourself
options.C: The Batches API, which manages agent loops for you
options.D: There is no difference; both are identical

questions.explanationCorrect: The Claude Agent SDK provides the agent harness (loop, tool execution, context handling) built on the API, while the raw Messages API gives you the primitives and you assemble the loop yourself.
questions.explanationDistractor: The raw Messages API (A) does not include a harness; you would have to write the loop, tool dispatch, and context handling manually.

questions.stem: Before sending a large request you want an accurate token count for the exact model and message shape you will use. What is the right approach?

options.A: Estimate with a generic tokenizer library like tiktoken
options.B: Divide the character count by four
options.C: Use the count_tokens endpoint, which counts for the actual model and request structure
options.D: Send the request and read usage afterward, since there is no way to count beforehand

questions.explanationCorrect: The count_tokens endpoint returns an accurate count for the specific model and request shape, which generic tokenizers cannot match.
questions.explanationDistractor: tiktoken (A) is a different provider's tokenizer and will not reflect Claude's tokenization; use the count_tokens endpoint instead.

questions.stem: You need Claude to answer questions about a multi-page PDF and a screenshot. How are these provided?

options.A: Only plain text extracted from them can be sent; native PDF and image input is unsupported
options.B: They must be uploaded to a separate vision product outside the Messages API
options.C: PDFs are supported but images are not
options.D: Both PDFs and images are supported as content blocks within a Messages API request (document and image inputs)

questions.explanationCorrect: The Messages API natively accepts PDF (document) and image inputs as content blocks, so you do not need to pre-extract text or use a separate product.
questions.explanationDistractor: Native PDF and vision input are supported (A is wrong), so pre-extracting text is unnecessary and would discard layout and visual information the model can use.

questions.stem: Claude requested three tools in a single turn. Your code returns each tool_result in its own separate user message across three API calls. Over time Claude stops calling tools in parallel. Why?

options.A: Splitting tool_results across multiple messages trains the model away from parallel calls; all tool_results for a turn should be returned together in one user message
options.B: Parallel tool use is only available on Haiku models
options.C: The tools' schemas must be merged into one combined schema
options.D: You must set tool_choice to any to keep parallelism

questions.explanationCorrect: All tool_results for a turn should be returned together in a single user message; splitting them across messages trains Claude to stop calling tools in parallel.
questions.explanationDistractor: Setting tool_choice to any (D) forces a tool call but does not fix the pattern; the remedy is returning all results together in one message.

questions.stem: How do you mark a block for caching, and what TTLs are available?

options.A: Set stream: true; caching is then automatic with a fixed 10-minute TTL
options.B: Add cache_control { type: "ephemeral" } to the block; the default TTL is 5 minutes, with a 1-hour option
options.C: Prefix the block with a special token; the TTL is always 24 hours
options.D: Enable it globally in the dashboard; the TTL cannot be changed

questions.explanationCorrect: You opt a block into caching with cache_control { type: "ephemeral" }; the default TTL is 5 minutes, and a 1-hour TTL is also available.
questions.explanationDistractor: Caching is not automatic and has no fixed 10-minute TTL (A); you opt in per block with cache_control and choose the TTL.

questions.stem: Your agent loop must handle every way a turn can end. Which set correctly lists Messages API stop_reason values you should branch on?

options.A: success, failure, retry, and timeout
options.B: complete, incomplete, and error
options.C: end_turn, tool_use, max_tokens, stop_sequence, plus pause_turn and refusal
options.D: done, continue, and stop

questions.explanationCorrect: Valid stop_reason values include end_turn, tool_use, max_tokens, stop_sequence, pause_turn (a server-tool loop paused), and refusal; the loop should branch on these.
questions.explanationDistractor: Options like success/failure/retry (A) are invented; the API reports structured stop_reason values such as end_turn and tool_use.

questions.stem: For a high-volume classification job where each item is simple and latency matters, which current model is the most cost-and-speed appropriate default, assuming quality is adequate?

options.A: Always use Opus 4.8 regardless of the task
options.B: Use whichever model has the largest context window
options.C: Fine-tune a custom model first
options.D: Haiku 4.5, which targets simple, high-throughput, latency-sensitive work (with Sonnet 5 as the balanced step up and Opus 4.8 for the hardest reasoning)

questions.explanationCorrect: Haiku 4.5 fits simple, high-volume, latency-sensitive tasks; Sonnet 5 is the balanced choice and Opus 4.8 is for the hardest reasoning. Match the model to the task.
questions.explanationDistractor: Defaulting everything to Opus (A) overpays and adds latency for simple, high-volume work that Haiku handles well.

questions.stem: On the newest models, how do you increase reasoning depth for a hard multi-step problem, given that fixed budget_tokens and sampling controls have changed?

options.A: Set a large budget_tokens value, exactly as before
options.B: Raise temperature so the model thinks harder
options.C: Use adaptive thinking (thinking type "adaptive") and set output_config.effort (low/medium/high/xhigh/max) to steer reasoning depth
options.D: There is no way to influence reasoning depth on current models

questions.explanationCorrect: Current models use adaptive thinking (replacing fixed budget_tokens) with an effort setting from low through max to control reasoning depth; temperature is not the lever.
questions.explanationDistractor: Fixed budget_tokens (A) has been superseded by adaptive thinking on the newest models; you steer depth with the effort setting instead.

questions.stem: After enabling prompt caching you want to confirm at runtime that reads are actually hitting the cache. What tells you?

options.A: The response latency alone proves it
options.B: A boolean 'cached' field on the message
options.C: The absence of any error means it worked
options.D: The usage object's cache_read_input_tokens (alongside the cache-creation fields) reported on the response

questions.explanationCorrect: The response usage reports cache_read_input_tokens (and cache-creation counts), which is the authoritative way to confirm caching is working.
questions.explanationDistractor: Latency (A) is noisy and not a reliable signal; the usage cache-token fields are what actually confirm a cache read.
